Oracle database found
 Potential 8
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 52
docker-compose.ymlLine 34
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 3
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 12
src/main/resources/application-docker.propertiesLine 6
src/main/resources/application.propertiesLine 15

Explanation

Oracle database found. To migrate a Java application that uses an Oracle database to Azure, you can follow these recommendations:

* Migrate to Azure Database for PostgreSQL: Azure recommends migrating Oracle databases to Azure Database for PostgreSQL Flexible Server as it provides better cost-effectiveness and performance. Create a managed PostgreSQL Flexible Server database in Azure and choose the appropriate pricing tier based on your application's requirements.

* Use migration tools: Utilize the Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or third-party tools to migrate your Oracle database schema and data to PostgreSQL. Consider using ora2pg or similar tools to convert Oracle-specific SQL to PostgreSQL-compatible SQL.

* Update database drivers and connection strings: Replace Oracle JDBC drivers with PostgreSQL drivers in your Java application. Update connection strings from Oracle format (jdbc:oracle:thin:) to PostgreSQL format (jdbc:postgresql:).

* Review and convert Oracle-specific code: Identify and convert Oracle-specific SQL functions, stored procedures, and PL/SQL code to PostgreSQL equivalents. Pay attention to data types, syntax differences, and built-in functions.

* Enable monitoring and diagnostics: Utilize Azure Monitor to gain insights into the performance and health of your Java application and the underlying PostgreSQL database. Set up metrics, alerts, and log analytics to proactively identify and resolve issues.

* Implement security measures: Apply security best practices to protect your Java application and the PostgreSQL database. This includes implementing authentication and authorization mechanisms with passwordless connections and leveraging Microsoft Defender for Cloud for threat detection and vulnerability assessments.

* Backup your data: Azure Database for PostgreSQL provides automated backups by default. You can configure the retention period for backups based on your requirements. You can also enable geo-redundant backups, if needed, to enhance data durability and availability.

Explanation

Using clear passwords in property files is a security risk, as they can be easily compromised if the files are accessed by unauthorized individuals. To enhance the security of your application, it is recommended to employ secure credential management practices.

* Azure Key Vault: Utilize Azure Key Vault to securely store and manage your application's passwords and other sensitive credentials. Azure Key Vault provides a centralized and highly secure location for storing secrets, keys, and certificates.

* Passwordless connections: You can provide an additional layer of security and convenience for accessing resources in Azure by eliminating the need for passwords. This way you can reduce the risk of password-related vulnerabilities, such as weak passwords or password theft.

If configured in configuration files: they will be ignored and overrided by Azure Container Apps.

If configured in Config Server files, command line parameters, Java system attribute, environment variable: they need to be removed or you might experience conflicts and unexpected behavior.

Detects usage of Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs
 Potential 5
FilePosition
pom.xmlLine 46

Explanation

The application depends on Jakarta Persistence (JPA) APIs (jakarta.persistence. or legacy javax.persistence.), which are used for object-relational mapping (ORM) and database interaction in Jakarta EE or Java EE applications.

When migrating to Azure:

  • Ensure that the database connection, JPA provider (e.g., Hibernate, EclipseLink), and dialect are compatible with your target Azure database service.
  • Recommended database services include Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for MySQL, or Azure SQL Database.
  • For containerized deployments, these JPA-based applications can run on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) or Azure App Service for Linux/Windows.
  • If using Spring Data JPA, verify that connection pool settings and environment variables are properly configured for the cloud environment.
  • Consider leveraging Azure Key Vault for secure storage of database credentials and connection strings.

CWE-606: Unchecked Input for Loop Condition
 Potential 3
File
src/main/java/com/photoalbum/controller/HomeController.java

Explanation

The product does not properly check inputs that are used for loop conditions, potentially leading to a denial of service or other consequences because of excessive looping.

Architecture Diagram

The application serves a browser-based photo gallery, accepts image uploads, and stores photo records and binary content in a relational database.

Application Architecture

flowchart TD subgraph Client["Client Layer"] Browser["Web Browser"] end subgraph Application["Application Layer - Spring Boot 3.5.0"] Web["Spring MVC and Thymeleaf"] Security["Spring Security HTTP Basic"] Controllers["Gallery, detail, and photo controllers"] Services["Photo service"] Repository["Spring Data JPA repository"] ORM["Hibernate ORM"] end subgraph Storage["Data Layer"] Oracle[("Oracle Database XE")] end Browser -->|"HTTP requests and image uploads"| Web Web --> Security Security -->|"authorized request"| Controllers Controllers -->|"photo operations"| Services Services -->|"CRUD and photo queries"| Repository Repository --> ORM ORM -->|"SQL and photo BLOB data"| Oracle

Technology Stack Summary

LayerTechnologyVersionPurpose
PresentationSpring MVC and ThymeleafSpring Boot 3.5.0Renders the gallery and photo detail pages and receives upload/delete requests
SecuritySpring SecurityManaged by Spring Boot 3.5.0Protects state-changing requests with stateless HTTP Basic authentication
Business logicSpring service componentsSpring Boot 3.5.0Validates image uploads, persists photos, and supports gallery navigation
PersistenceSpring Data JPA and HibernateHibernate 6.6.15.FinalRepository access and ORM mapping
DatabaseOracle Database XE21.3.0-xe in ComposeStores photo metadata and binary content

Data Storage & External Services

Oracle Database XE is the only application data store. The Photo entity keeps image bytes in a database LOB; no cache, message broker, or external application API was identified.

Key Architectural Decisions

  • Uses Spring MVC controllers, a service layer, and a Spring Data JPA repository.
  • Stores uploaded images in the database rather than on the application filesystem.
  • Uses server-rendered Thymeleaf pages alongside a JSON response for uploads.

DTOs & Contracts

UploadResult is a mutable service-level result object used to carry upload outcome information. The upload controller shapes its HTTP response using maps rather than a dedicated immutable response DTO. Photo is the service-owned persistence entity used by gallery and detail flows; see data-architecture.md for its model. No OpenAPI/Swagger, protobuf, or GraphQL contract files were found. Spring Boot uses Jackson for JSON serialization.

Communication Patterns

  • Controllers synchronously call PhotoService; PhotoServiceImpl synchronously calls PhotoRepository, which accesses Oracle through JPA/Hibernate.
  • No asynchronous messaging, circuit breaker, retry policy, service discovery, or API gateway was identified.
  • Docker Compose starts the application after the Oracle service reports healthy; startup and configuration details are in configuration-inventory.md.
  • HTTP Basic authentication is configured for POST upload and deletion requests. Read-only gallery and photo retrieval requests are permitted anonymously. HTTPS/TLS is not configured in the application or Compose definition.

Core Business Workflows

Photo Album lets users browse a gallery, upload image files, view full-size photos, navigate between neighboring photos, and delete stored photos.

Domain Entities

EntityService / Bounded ContextDescriptionKey Relationships
PhotoPhoto Album / Photo CatalogA user-uploaded image together with its display metadata and stored contentNo other domain entity relationships identified

Service-to-Domain Mapping

ServiceDomain ContextOwned EntitiesExternal Dependencies
Photo Album applicationPhoto CatalogPhotoOracle database

Primary Workflows

Workflow 1: Upload photos

  1. An authenticated user submits one or more files through the gallery upload form.
  2. HomeController iterates through submitted files and invokes PhotoServiceImpl.
  3. The service checks the MIME type, file size, and whether the file is empty. It reads the content, extracts image header dimensions when possible, and rejects images exceeding the 40-million-pixel limit.
  4. The service creates a Photo and saves it through PhotoRepository; the controller returns JSON with successful uploads and failures.

Business rules include an allowed MIME list of JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP, a 10 MiB file limit, and the maximum image pixel count. A max-files-per-upload=10 setting is declared but is not enforced by the controller.

Workflow 2: Browse and view photos

  1. A visitor opens the gallery. The application retrieves photos ordered by upload time and renders the page.
  2. A visitor opens a detail page for a photo. The application retrieves that photo and requests older/newer records for navigation.
  3. The photo content route retrieves the stored bytes and returns them using the recorded MIME type; missing photos or empty content produce a not-found response.

Workflow 3: Delete a photo

  1. An authenticated user submits a delete request for a photo identifier.
  2. The service looks up the photo, returns not-found behavior if absent, or deletes it from the database.
  3. The browser is redirected to the gallery with a success or error message.

Cross-Service Data Flows

There are no independently deployed application services to aggregate. The application service uses its repository to read and write Oracle-backed photo records; image bytes are stored in the Photo record rather than a separate object-storage service.

Business Workflow Sequence

sequenceDiagram participant User participant Security as "Spring Security" participant Gallery as "HomeController" participant Service as "PhotoService" participant Repository as "PhotoRepository" participant Database as "Oracle Database" User->>Security: Submit photo upload with credentials Security->>Security: Verify HTTP Basic credentials alt Authenticated Security->>Gallery: Accept upload request loop Each submitted file Gallery->>Service: Process image Service->>Service: Check MIME, size, emptiness, and dimensions alt File passes checks Service->>Repository: Save photo and bytes Repository->>Database: Persist photo Database-->>Repository: Stored photo Repository-->>Service: Save result Service-->>Gallery: Upload success else File rejected or save fails Service-->>Gallery: Upload failure details end end Gallery-->>User: Upload result summary else Not authenticated Security-->>User: Authentication challenge end

Business Rules & Decision Logic

  • Uploads must use an allowed image MIME type, have non-empty content, and not exceed the configured per-file size. When dimensions can be extracted, uploads above 40 million pixels are rejected.
  • Individual file processing failures are returned in the upload result; successful files are persisted independently.
  • The configured per-request file count is 10, but the code does not currently enforce that setting.
  • Gallery ordering is newest-first; detail navigation finds older and newer photos by upload timestamp.
  • Upload and delete operations require authentication. Gallery viewing and photo retrieval are public.
  • PhotoServiceImpl is transactionally scoped, with read-only annotations on retrieval operations. No cross-service saga or audit trail was identified.

Version & Compatibility Risks

Spring Boot 3.5.0 and Java 21 are explicit project targets. Apache Commons IO 2.14.0 is independently versioned and should be tracked separately from the Spring Boot-managed dependencies. The Oracle JDBC driver is runtime-scoped and its resolved version is 23.7.0.25.01.

Notable Observations

  • The Spring Boot parent POM manages versions for most Spring, Hibernate, and test dependencies.
  • spring-boot-starter-json overlaps with JSON support already brought in by the web starter.
  • The application uses Oracle-specific SQL, so database-driver replacement alone would not establish portability.

erDiagram Photo { string Id PK string OriginalFileName bytes PhotoData long FileSize string MimeType datetime UploadedAt int Width int Height }

The entity stores the original name, image bytes, size, MIME type, upload timestamp, and optional dimensions. It has validation annotations for required values, positive file size, and bounded name/MIME length. PhotoServiceImpl is transactionally scoped; retrieval methods are read-only.

Caching Strategy

No application cache, cache annotations, cache provider, or Hibernate second-level cache configuration was detected.

Data Ownership Boundaries

The single application service owns its data in one shared Oracle schema. All read and write operations pass through PhotoServiceImpl and PhotoRepository; there are no cross-service database access patterns, event flows, or CQRS boundaries. The native SQL uses Oracle-specific constructs, including NVL, ROWNUM, SYSDATE, and DUAL.
